details:
**Booms and busts**
The alternating periods of economic expansion and contraction that make up the business cycle, which is why it is also called the "boom and bust cycle." This is the most common giveaway.

**Peaks, troughs, expansions, and recessions**
The phases of a business cycle. Output and employment rise during an expansion, top out at a peak, fall during a recession or contraction, and bottom out at a trough before recovery begins.

**Real business cycle theory (Kydland and Prescott)**
A model developed by Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott that explains business cycles as efficient responses to persistent technology or productivity shocks. It implies that monetary policy is ineffective at smoothing the cycle. The two won the 2004 Nobel Prize in Economics partly for this work.

**Burns and Mitchell's Measuring Business Cycles**
A 1946 book by Arthur Burns and Wesley Mitchell that set the standard method for identifying business cycles. It anchored the National Bureau of Economic Research's work on dating them.

**National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)**
The private U.S. research organization whose Business Cycle Dating Committee officially determines when U.S. recessions and expansions begin and end. Most people use its dates.

**Joseph Schumpeter and creative destruction**
The Austrian-born economist Joseph Schumpeter argued that business cycles are driven by waves of innovation, in which new technologies and firms destroy old ones. He called this process "creative destruction."

**Ragnar Frisch's impulse and propagation**
Ragnar Frisch, who shared the first Nobel Prize in Economics, modeled cycles as random "impulses" (shocks) passed through an economy's "propagation mechanism," which turns them into regular oscillations. He compared this to a rocking horse being struck.

**The Great Moderation**
The period from the mid-1980s until the 2007–2008 financial crisis when business-cycle volatility in the U.S. and other developed economies was unusually low, leading many economists to believe cycles had been largely tamed.

**Robert Lucas's welfare cost calculation**
In his 1987 book Models of Business Cycles, Robert Lucas calculated that the welfare cost of business-cycle fluctuations to the average consumer is very small, close to zero, compared with the gains from faster long-run growth.

**Hodrick-Prescott filter**
A statistical tool used to separate the short-term cyclical part of a time series (such as GDP) from its long-run trend, so economists can isolate business-cycle fluctuations.

**Kondratiev waves**
Very long cycles of roughly 50 years in economic activity, proposed by the Soviet economist Nikolai Kondratiev, offered as an alternative or addition to ordinary business cycles.

**Irving Fisher's debt deflation**
Irving Fisher's 1933 theory of depressions, in which over-indebtedness leads to distress selling and falling prices. The falling prices raise the real burden of debt and deepen the downturn.

**Austrian business cycle theory**
The Austrian School, associated with Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, argues that artificially low interest rates set by central banks cause overinvestment and malinvestment during booms, which then must be corrected in busts.
